Policy Statement

NWS has a zero-tolerance approach to fraud, bribery and corruption and will take all appropriate measures to prevent and detect it. The facilitation of tax evasion, and money laundering are also strictly prohibited.

Failure to comply with this Policy will be a disciplinary matter which will be considered under the NWS Disciplinary Policy. The leadership of NWS is determined that the culture and tone of the organisation is one of honesty and an intolerance of fraud, bribery, and corruption.

We are committed to:

developing a strong culture of integrity across the organisation.

having ‘adequate procedures’, including effective systems, processes and controls in place to prevent fraud, bribery and corruption and other financial crimes.

the proper use of funds, both public and private.

taking all reports of fraud, bribery and corruption and other financial crimes seriously and investigating them proportionally and appropriately.

seeking the appropriate disciplinary, regulatory, civil and criminal sanctions against those who commit fraud, bribery and corruption and, where applicable, recovering losses.

In line with the NWS Code of Conduct and reflecting the Nolan Principles of Public life all staff have a responsibility to assist in preventing fraud, bribery and corruption.

We recognise that fraud, bribery and corruption can:

Undermine the standards of public service that NWS seeks to achieve.

Reduce the resources available to NWS to achieve our strategic objectives.

Have major consequences which reduce public confidence and affect the reputation of NWS.

This Policy applies to all NWS staff, regardless of position held and employment type, including non-executive directors, executive directors, permanent and interim workers (ASW’s and CSW’s) and secondees, as well as consultants and contractors. We also expect all suppliers and any other party who has a professional or business relationship with us to align to these principles.

Our approach to protecting NWS from the risk of fraud, bribery and corruption is a multi-faceted, risk-based approach, which includes risk assessment, prevention, deterrence, detection, measurement, investigation, and sanctions. This Policy is underpinned by a Fraud, Bribery and Corruption Strategy which sets out what actions NWS takes to continue to develop its resilience to fraud, bribery, and corruption.

1. Context

The purpose of this Policy is to set out key elements of our approach to managing the risk of fraud, bribery or corruption and other related unethical behaviour risks, in line with our Fraud, Bribery and Corruption Strategy. It also sets out the key roles and responsibilities, as well as specifically what is required of all employees.

This Policy is prepared in accordance with Government Functional Standard GovS 013: Counter Frauda and relates to all forms of fraud, bribery, and corruption, as defined in Section 2 below. The Standard sets the expectations for the management of fraud, bribery, and corruption activity in government organisations, and includes the requirement to undertake risk assessments for our exposure to fraud as a business, and at a programme and project level.

The aim of the Policy is to ensure all concerns raised are captured, considered, and dealt with appropriately. It will also help us to learn from the matters that are raised so that we can improve how the NDA Group operates as part of our vision to create great places to work. It is not contractual; we will review it regularly and may change it.

The NDA as a Group entity is required to report to DESNZ annually our compliance against GovS 013 at the Group level; NWS data is consolidated within this submission. A subsequent annual action plan is developed to address any weaknesses in our processes, identified either through the compliance self-assessment, assurance activities or lessons learnt exercises following investigations. Progress against this action plan is monitored by the Audit and Risk Assurance Committee (ARAC).

2. Definitions and Examples

Fraud essentially involves using deception to dishonestly make a personal gain for oneself and/or create a loss for another. This can include theft, the misuse of funds or other resources, or more complicated crimes such as false accounting and the supply of false information. Definitions are included to provide clarity as to what this Policy is concerned with. Where examples are given, these are not intended to be exhaustive.

Fraud is the intentional use of deception to gain a financial advantage or to deprive, disadvantage or cause loss to another.

This can include the misuse of funds or other resources and/or the supply of false information. The focus is on the dishonest behaviour of the subject and their intent to make a financial gain or cause a financial loss. The gain or loss does not have to succeed if the intent is there.

There are 3 main fraud offences under the Fraud Act 2006:

Section 2 – Fraud by false representation – for example, falsely making expense claims, or exaggerating hours on timesheets.

Section 3 – Fraud by failing to disclose – for example, not disclosing unspent criminal convictions to gain employment.

Section 4 – Fraud by abuse of position – for example, intentionally abusing delegations of authority.

Other examples may include:

working for another employer whilst on sickness absence,

suppliers submitting payment claims for goods or services that were not delivered or inferior to what was specified in the order (invoice fraud), or

requesting a change to staff or supplier payment details to their own (mandate fraud).

Arrangements may be made to recover losses via payroll if the subject is still employed by NWS. In all cases, current legislation must be complied with. It should be noted that the duty to follow disciplinary procedures will not override any requirement to take legal action in the case of suspected fraud, bribery or corruption, and legal requirements shall prevail.

The civil recovery route is also available if this is cost-effective and desirable for deterrence purposes. This could involve a number of options such as applying for reimbursement through the Small Claims Court and/or recovery through debt collection agencies. Each case needs to be discussed with the Chief Financial Officer and the General Counsel/Company Secretary, to determine the most appropriate action.

Criminal investigations are primarily used for dealing with any criminal activity. The main purpose is to determine if activity was undertaken with criminal intent. Following such an investigation, it may be necessary to bring this activity to the attention of the criminal courts (magistrates court and Crown court). Outcomes can range from fines to imprisonment.

Redress allows resources that are lost to fraud and bribery to be returned to the public purse use as intended. Depending on the extent of the loss and the proceedings in the case, it may be suitable for the recovery of losses to be considered under the Proceeds of Crime Act 2002 (POCA). This means that a person’s money or assets can be taken away from them if it is believed that they benefited from the crime. It could also include restraining assets during the course of the investigation. When considering seeking redress, recovery may also be sought from ongoing salary payments or pensions.”

6. Lessons Learnt

NWS is committed to ensuring that opportunities for fraud, bribery and corruption are reduced to the lowest possible level of risk. In the event that fraud, bribery, corruption, or unethical behaviour is discovered, NWS will take steps to ensure lessons learnt from the event are applied to existing policies and practices. This might include implementing changes to the existing system of controls, increasing awareness of the risk of fraud and/or bribery, disseminating lessons learnt where there may be implications for the wider organisation.
